claims.statement: Gonadorelin is the synthetic form of native hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH/LHRH), a decapeptide that acts on the anterior pituitary to stimulate release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH).

extractedEvidence.quote: Gonadorelin is used to test how well the hypothalamus and the pituitary glands are working.
Factrel (gonadorelin) has been shown to have gonadotropin-releasing effects upon the anterior pituitary.

reviewFlags: independently confirmed 2026-08-29 via RxList reproduction of the historical FDA-derived human Factrel label, closing the prior regulator-source gap for this mechanism claim

claims.statement: The only current FDA-approved gonadorelin product identified on DailyMed (FACTREL, gonadorelin hydrochloride injection) is an FDA-approved veterinary drug for cattle - indicated for treatment of ovarian follicular cysts and for estrous-cycle synchronization - and its label explicitly states it is not approved for human use.

context.population: cattle (lactating dairy cows, beef cows, replacement heifers)
context.doseText: 2 mL single IM injection for cystic ovaries; 2-4 mL (100-200 mcg) IM per cow in fixed-time AI synchronization protocol (label text, veterinary product; not a human dosing reference)

extractedEvidence.quote: For use in animals only. Not for human use. Keep out of reach of children.
Federal law restricts this drug to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian.

CYSTORELIN (Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health USA Inc.); FACTREL (Zoetis Inc.); FERTAGYL (Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp.); GONABREED (Parnell Technologies Pty Ltd); OVACYST (Bimeda, Inc.) -- all identified as animal drugs.
The brand name Factrel is discontinued, but generic versions may be available.

reviewFlags: RESOLVED 2026-08-29: live DailyMed search confirms exactly five gonadorelin products, all veterinary; RxList independently confirms the historical human Factrel product is discontinued in the US (no active human gonadorelin product identified) -- no current US human gonadorelin product exists, consistent with this claim's veterinary-only characterization

claims.statement: In Canada, LUTREPULSE (gonadorelin acetate, delivered via pulsatile subcutaneous pump) is indicated per its Health Canada product monograph for induction of ovulation in women with primary hypothalamic amenorrhea; this ovulation-induction indication is Canada-specific and historical, not a currently active US indication (the corresponding human Factrel product in the US is confirmed discontinued). Gonadorelin has also historically been used diagnostically, under a since-discontinued US FDA-approved human product, to test hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis function.

context.doseText: starting dose 5 mcg every 90 minutes SC via pulsatile pump (Health Canada product monograph text; not a use recommendation)

extractedEvidence.quote: LUTREPULSE (gonadorelin acetate) is indicated for the induction of ovulation in women with primary hypothalamic amenorrhea.
The recommended starting dose in primary hypothalamic amenorrhea is 5 µg every 90 minutes, administered SC.
It is also used to cause ovulation (release of an egg from the ovary) in women who do not have regular ovulation and menstrual periods because the hypothalamus gland does not release enough GnRH.
The brand name Factrel is discontinued, but generic versions may be available.

reviewFlags: product-specific dosing claim - Canadian product monograph, not a US label; confirm whether an equivalent human product currently holds US marketing authorization
this indication is unrelated to gray-market TRT-adjunct use and must not be conflated with it

RESOLVED (wording) 2026-08-29: statement reworded to explicitly mark the ovulation-induction indication as Canada-only/historical per independent review finding; RxList independently confirms the corresponding US human Factrel product is discontinued. The ovulation-induction indication's current Canadian marketing status was not itself re-verified this session (2016 monograph is the only source) and remains a narrower residual gap for review

claims.statement: Regulator/clinical-reference sources warn that gonadorelin use is contraindicated or hazardous in patients with hormone-dependent tumors (risk the tumor may worsen) and in undiagnosed gonadotropin-releasing-hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma, where treatment could precipitate pituitary complications including sudden vision loss; ovarian hyperstimulation and multiple pregnancy are recognized risks of pulsatile use for ovulation induction.

context.population: patients with hormone-dependent tumors, undiagnosed pituitary adenoma, or ovarian cysts; women undergoing ovulation induction

extractedEvidence.quote: Although this condition is rare, use of gonadorelin when this condition exists may cause problems in the pituitary gland and could result in sudden blindness
The increase of estrogens and progestins in women or androgens in men...may make a tumor worse if the tumor depends on estrogens, progestins, or androgens for growth.
Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a known risk with ovulation induction therapies, but is rare with pulsatile GnRH therapy.
any condition that could be exacerbated by pregnancy
There has been a report of pituitary apoplexy and sudden blindness following gonadotropin-releasing hormone administration to a patient with a gonadotropin-secreting adenoma.

The increase of estrogens and progestins in women or androgens in men that can result from use of multiple doses of gonadorelin may make a tumor worse if the tumor depends on estrogens, progestins, or androgens for growth

reviewFlags: RESOLVED 2026-08-29: independently confirmed by RxList's reproduction of the US FDA-derived human Factrel label (pituitary apoplexy/sudden blindness warning, verbatim) and by Drugs.com (hormone-dependent tumor worsening warning), closing the prior gap where this claim was sourced only from a Canadian monograph and Mayo/Micromedex

claims.statement: In a prospective, self-selected open-label comparison in 28 azoospermic men with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH), pulsatile subcutaneous gonadorelin (10 mcg every 90 minutes via infusion pump) induced spermatogenesis significantly earlier than cyclical hCG/hMG therapy (median 6 vs 14 months), though overall spermatogenesis-success rates were statistically similar between the two approaches (90% vs 83.3%).

context.population: azoospermic men aged 16-34 with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH), n=28 (not randomized - self-selected treatment arm)
context.useCase: fertility induction in CHH (a distinct, pump-dependent medical condition - not TRT-adjunct use)
context.doseText: 10 mcg every 90 minutes via subcutaneous infusion pump, followed over 24 months (trial protocol; not a use recommendation)

extractedEvidence.quote: The pulsatile group received subcutaneous gonadorelin 10 μg every 90 minutes using an infusion pump.
Spermatogenesis appeared significantly earlier in the pulsatile group at median of 6 and 14 months, respectively (χ2 = 6.711, p = .01).
Overall success rates were comparable: 90% in the pulsatile group versus 83.3% in the cyclical group, without statistically significant differences.
the 6.48±1.84 months sperm emergence time shown in this study is significantly shorter than the 9–18 months reported in hCG studies
The sperm production rate of 79.4% in this study is slightly better than the 75.8% and 76.9% rates reported in multiple hCG studies.

reviewFlags: study population (CHH, requiring a mechanical pulsatile pump) is not equivalent to men on exogenous testosterone therapy with an intact hypothalamic-pituitary axis; do not extrapolate to gray-market TRT-adjunct dosing
treatment arm was self-selected, not randomized - confounding possible

RESOLVED 2026-08-29: an independent, separate primary study (Jiang et al., PMC12336735, different authors/cohort than Zhang 2019) was fetched and corroborates the same qualitative finding -- pulsatile GnRH pump therapy produces faster spermatogenesis onset (6.48 vs 9-18 months) and comparable-or-better success rate (79.4% vs 75.8-76.9%) versus hCG/gonadotropin therapy. This is not an exact replication of Zhang 2019's specific figures (6 vs 14 months; 90% vs 83.3%) but independently supports the same direction of effect; the original Zhang 2019 primary PMC full text itself remains reCAPTCHA-blocked and was not independently re-pulled this session

authority-flag recalibrated 2026-08-29: claimType studied-use is outside the directive's fieldAuthorityRequired scope; claim reports peer-reviewed findings at source-level attribution ("In a prospective, self-selected open-label comparison in 28 azoospermic men with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH)..."); no regulator document exists for this claim (searched: FDA.gov and DailyMed for gonadorelin human products and any spermatogenesis/CHH indication - DailyMed lists only 5 veterinary gonadorelin products (CYSTORELIN, FACTREL, FERTAGYL, GONABREED, OVACYST), none addressing human fertility or spermatogenesis induction; no current FDA-approved human gonadorelin product or label was located)

claims.statement: Gonadorelin is widely marketed by telehealth/TRT clinics as a lower-cost hCG alternative to prevent testicular shrinkage and preserve fertility during testosterone replacement therapy, but no controlled human trial data specific to that TRT-adjunct use (intermittent/non-pulsatile subcutaneous dosing in men on exogenous testosterone) was located this session; the clinic source itself concedes evidence is thin and that fertility preservation should not be assumed.

context.population: men on testosterone replacement therapy seeking fertility/testicular-size preservation
context.route: subcutaneous (commonly marketed use, dosing schedules vary by clinic)
context.useCase: TRT-adjunct marketing claim (testicular size / fertility preservation) - distinct from the FDA/Health Canada-approved diagnostic and ovulation-induction indications

extractedEvidence.quote: gonadorelin should not be assumed to have preserved your fertility
the response is not reliable enough to promise in advance
maintaining testicular size does not prove that sperm production, fertility, or long-term testicular functional capacity have been preserved

reviewFlags: misinformation-adjacent: popular TRT-clinic marketing claims (testicular-size and fertility preservation) lack supporting controlled human outcome trials specific to this use and dosing pattern
no product used for this purpose has any current FDA approval; compounded/gray-market sourcing implicated
distinguish clearly from the CHH pulsatile-pump spermatogenesis-induction evidence, which is a different population, mechanism-consistent but not directly transferable

independently re-checked 2026-08-29: attempted to fetch a potentially relevant controlled trial (Fertility and Sterility, low-dose hCG for fertility preservation during TRT, https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(10)01624-9/fulltext) to test whether it changes the gap characterization; the page returned a 403 error this session and could not be independently read, so no quote from it was added. That trial concerns hCG, not gonadorelin, so its inaccessibility does not affect this claim's evidence-gap conclusion -- no controlled trial of gonadorelin specifically for this TRT-adjunct use was located, and the evidence-gap statement stands unchanged

context.formulation: gonadorelin base and salt forms (acetate, diacetate, hydrochloride)

reviewFlags: CAS number 33515-09-2 obtained via PubChem PUG-View CAS section during this session; independently confirmed 2026-08-29 against two independent chemical registries (ChemicalBook, Alfa Chemistry), both matching CAS 33515-09-2 to gonadorelin (free-base form)

RESIDUAL GAP (kept open per independent review): neither ChemicalBook nor Alfa Chemistry independently confirmed a distinct CAS number for the acetate salt form this session (Alfa Chemistry explicitly lists only the single base-form CAS with no separate salt-form number) -- do not state a specific acetate-salt CAS number until independently verified against a fetched page; DrugBank/ChEMBL numeric cross-reference (CAS, formula, IDs) also remains unconfirmed from their native databases this session

conflicts.summary: Only veterinary gonadorelin products (FACTREL and four others, confirmed via a live DailyMed search 2026-08-29) are currently listed on US DailyMed; a human indication (LUTREPULSE, ovulation induction) is documented only via a Canadian Health Canada product monograph. RxList independently confirms 2026-08-29 that the historical US human Factrel product is discontinued, resolving the narrow question of whether a human gonadorelin product is currently US-marketed (it is not). The claim wording has been updated to state the ovulation-induction indication is Canada-only/historical. Residual open question: whether LUTREPULSE remains currently active in Canada was not independently re-verified this session (source is a 2016 monograph).

reviewReasons: Expansion-batch evidence packet requires human review before publication.

RESOLVED 2026-08-29 (veterinary/human-US split): live DailyMed search confirms exactly 5 gonadorelin products, all veterinary, and RxList independently confirms the historical human Factrel product is discontinued in the US -- no current US human gonadorelin product exists. The Canada-only LUTREPULSE ovulation-induction indication (gonadorelin-approved-indication-human-historical-001) has been reworded to make this explicit; whether LUTREPULSE remains currently active in Canada itself was not independently re-verified this session (source is a 2016 monograph) and is a narrower residual item for reviewer spot-check.

PubMed/PMC primary-literature pages were blocked by bot-verification (reCAPTCHA) during this session for the original Zhang 2019 article; an independent, separate primary study (Jiang et al., PMC12336735, fetched successfully 2026-08-29) corroborates the same qualitative CHH spermatogenesis finding and has been added as a second citation. The Zhang 2019 primary full text itself (exact 6-vs-14-month, 90%-vs-83.3% figures) remains unverified against PMC directly and should still be pulled at review if those exact figures need primary-source confirmation.

No controlled human trial specific to gray-market TRT-adjunct dosing (testicular size/fertility preservation while on exogenous testosterone) was found; a candidate hCG (not gonadorelin) trial in Fertility and Sterility was attempted this session (https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(10)01624-9/fulltext) but returned a 403 error and could not be independently read -- this remains an evidence gap rather than a resolved question, and the claim language is unchanged since it already asserts no more than the absence of trials.

DrugBank/ChEMBL/UNII identifiers not independently confirmed from their native databases this session. Independent chemical registries (ChemicalBook, Alfa Chemistry) confirmed 2026-08-29 that CAS 33515-09-2 matches gonadorelin base form, but neither surfaced a distinct salt-form (e.g., acetate) CAS number, so no specific acetate-salt CAS figure has been added to the packet -- DrugBank/ChEMBL/UNII should still be pulled directly from their native databases at review time to close this gap fully.
